data.name: Squareboy vs Bullies: Arena Edition
data.detailed_description:
Wishlist Devious Dungeon 2


Acerca do jogo

Alguém precisa de dar a esses Bullies uma lição de dor, que tal seres tu a fazê-lo?

Squareboy versus Bullies é uma velha escola tentar derrotá-los por Rohan Narang que segue o personagem Squareboy e a sua procura por justiça!

Durante demasiado tempo, os bullies ficaram impunes e sem ninguém para os pôr na ordem, Squareboy insurge-se contra eles para fazer o que está correto, não apenas por si mesmo, mas por toda a gente que os bullies vitimizaram. Vais ajudar o Squareboy a lutar contra os Bullies?

Características
  • Imagens de arte píxel retro e OST com 14 faixas de chiptune diferentes.
  • Luta em vários locais diferentes em Squareburg.
  • Novo modo Arena.
  • Bullies nunca antes vistos.
  • Novo ecrã UI que aproveita todo o espaço do ecrã.

reviews.review:
Squareboy vs Bullies: Arena Edition is a compact old-school beat 'em up that understands exactly what kind of experience it wants to deliver. Instead of complicating its action with elaborate progression trees, equipment management, or lengthy storytelling, it focuses on walking through colorful environments and beating up groups of troublemakers. Developed by Rohan Narang and Ratalaika Games S.L. and published by Ratalaika Games S.L., it has the spirit of a small arcade brawler designed for players who value immediate action over mechanical complexity.

The story is deliberately straightforward. Squareboy lives in Squareburg, where bullies have been causing trouble without facing consequences. Rather than continuing to tolerate their behavior, he decides to fight back, not only for himself but also for everyone else they have victimized. There is little emphasis on sophisticated characterization or dramatic storytelling, but the uncomplicated premise suits the arcade structure. The player always understands the objective, and the game wastes little time before placing another collection of enemies in the way.

Combat follows traditional 2D beat 'em up conventions. Players move around the battlefield, attack approaching enemies, avoid becoming surrounded, and gradually clear each encounter before advancing. The controls and mechanics are intentionally accessible, making the game easy to understand even for someone who has little experience with the genre. There is a pleasant simplicity to jumping into a fight without needing to memorize complicated systems. At the same time, that accessibility exposes the game's biggest limitation. Its fighting mechanics do not possess enough depth to keep every encounter feeling substantially different, so repetition becomes increasingly apparent once the initial novelty has passed.

Enemy variety helps compensate to some degree. Different bullies appear throughout the adventure, while the changing locations around Squareburg provide visual separation between confrontations. The Arena Edition also expands the basic concept with additional opponents and an Arena mode. Arena is particularly appropriate because the game's strongest quality is its immediate combat. Removing much of the surrounding progression and concentrating on surviving fights provides another reason to return after completing the main journey. It does not fundamentally transform the mechanics, but it gives players who enjoy the basic fighting system a more focused environment in which to continue using it.

The visual presentation is firmly rooted in retro gaming. Pixel graphics give the characters and environments a deliberately simple appearance, and the art remains readable when several characters occupy the screen. It is not an especially elaborate demonstration of modern pixel artistry, but the straightforward look complements the arcade-inspired design. A redesigned interface also makes better use of the display compared with the game's earlier presentation. The soundtrack strengthens the nostalgic atmosphere considerably, offering 14 chiptune tracks that match the energetic, uncomplicated nature of the action. Together, the graphics and music create an identity reminiscent of portable and arcade games from earlier generations without becoming excessively concerned with visual spectacle.

The overall amount of mechanical variety is where expectations need to remain reasonable. Players who approach the game expecting the elaborate combo possibilities, progression systems, branching character builds, or extensive replay incentives associated with larger modern brawlers may find it rather limited. Much of the experience revolves around variations of the same fundamental activity, and its straightforward enemy encounters eventually reveal how small the underlying combat system really is. On the other hand, that same simplicity makes it suitable for short sessions. There is very little preparation required, and returning after a break does not involve relearning complicated controls or remembering numerous interconnected mechanics.

Several supporting Steam features make the package slightly more attractive for completion-oriented players. There are 26 achievements to pursue alongside Steam Cloud support and Family Sharing. The achievements provide additional objectives beyond merely reaching the end, while the Arena mode gives players another place to continue fighting. Partial controller support is indicated in current Steam metadata, so players expecting completely seamless controller integration should keep that qualification in mind.

Steam Deck compatibility requires a more cautious assessment. The Steam store does not currently provide an official Steam Deck compatibility rating for the game, while SteamDB lists Windows as its supported operating system and identifies controller support as partial. Consequently, it should not be described as officially Steam Deck Verified or Playable. The modest nature of the game suggests that raw hardware performance is unlikely to be the primary concern, but compatibility through SteamOS and Proton, controller behavior, and any required adjustments cannot be guaranteed from the official information currently available. Anyone specifically purchasing it for Steam Deck should therefore treat it as an unverified title rather than assuming completely trouble-free handheld operation.

What ultimately makes the experience appealing is its lack of pretension. It wants to provide a quick dose of pixelated brawling, a lighthearted battle against cartoon bullies, catchy chiptune music, and enough different environments to carry its uncomplicated adventure. It accomplishes those objectives reasonably well. The tradeoff is that there simply is not enough mechanical sophistication for the fighting to remain consistently fresh over extended play. The Arena additions improve replay value, but they cannot entirely compensate for limited combat depth.

As a result, this is best viewed as a modest retro diversion rather than an essential modern beat 'em up. Players nostalgic for simple arcade action may enjoy its directness, charming presentation, and easy-to-understand fighting, while those seeking deep combos and extensive progression are likely to come away wanting more. Its simplicity can simultaneously be considered its greatest strength and its most obvious weakness, producing an accessible game that is entertaining in shorter bursts but struggles to develop significantly beyond its initial concept.

Rating: 6/10
